hints: Think about what happens to the concentration of a reactant if it starts in huge excess compared to the others, how much does it actually fall during the reaction?
walkthrough:
Picture the isolation trick**
Imagine you want to see how $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ and $\text{H}^+$ affect rate, but $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ is also changing. That is messy. If you flood the mixture with $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$, the small amount that reacts is tiny compared to what you started with.

Link to constant concentration**
Because the percentage change in $[\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3]$ is negligible, it behaves as a constant during the experiment. Its effect is folded into the rate constant, so any change in initial rate must be due only to $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]$ and $[\text{H}^+]$. This is the isolation method.
Final answer: A large excess of $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ is used so its concentration stays almost constant and does not affect the measured rate.

hints: Compare experiments 2 and 3 where $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]$ is fixed, work out the factor change in $[\text{H}^+]$ and in rate.
Compare experiments 1 and 2 where both $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]$ and $[\text{H}^+]$ change by 1.5, use your result for $\text{H}^+$ to isolate the effect of $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$.
walkthrough:
Isolate the effect of $\text{H}^+$**
Look at experiments 2 and 3. $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]$ is held at $0.015 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. $[\text{H}^+]$ goes $0.015 \to 0.020$, a factor of $0.020/0.015 = 4/3$. Rate goes $2.25 \to 3.00$, also a factor of $3.00/2.25 = 4/3$. Same factor change means rate is directly proportional to $[\text{H}^+]$, so first order in $\text{H}^+$.

Untangle the combined change**
Now look at experiments 1 and 2. $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]$ goes $0.010 \to 0.015$ ($\times 1.5$) and $[\text{H}^+]$ goes $0.010 \to 0.015$ ($\times 1.5$). Rate goes $1.00 \to 2.25$ ($\times 2.25$). Since you already know $\text{H}^+$ contributes a factor of $1.5$, the remaining factor $2.25/1.5 = 1.5$ must come from $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$. So rate $\propto [\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]^1$, first order in $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$.

Final answer: Order w.r.t. $\text{H}^+$ is 1: expts 2 to 3, $[\text{H}^+]$ $\times$ 4/3 (0.015 to 0.020) and rate $\times$ 4/3 (2.25 to 3.00).
Order w.r.t. $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ is 1: expts 1 to 2, $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]$ $\times$ 1.5, $[\text{H}^+]$ $\times$ 1.5 and rate $\times$ 2.25 $= 1.5^2$, consistent with first order in each.

hints: For a first order reactant under isolation conditions, what feature of the decay curve stays the same all the way along, think about time to halve?
walkthrough:
Use the half-life test**
Under these conditions $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ and $\text{H}^+$ are in excess, so only $[\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3]$ falls significantly. For a first order decay, the time to halve should be independent of starting concentration.

Read values off Fig. 2.2**
Start at 100% at $t = 0$. It reaches 50% at about $t = 160 \text{ s}$. From 50%, halve again to 25% at about $t = 320 \text{ s}$. That second half-life is $320 - 160 = 160 \text{ s}$. Two half-lives both about $155$ to $170 \text{ s}$ and roughly constant proves first order behaviour.
Final answer: Successive half-lives are approximately constant, about 160 s, e.g. 100% to 50% in approx 160 s and 50% to 25% in approx 160 s, showing first order in $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$.

hints: Recall that only species involved in or before the slow, rate determining step can appear in the rate equation.
Check the given rate equation $\text{rate} = k[\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3][\text{H}^+]$, which species must be in the slow step and which must not be?
Compare the mole ratio in the slow step with the powers in the rate equation to narrow down to one mechanism.
walkthrough:
Remember what controls rate**
Think of the mechanism as a bottleneck. The slow step is the bottleneck, so the experimental rate law is set by what collides in that slow step. Any reactant that appears after the slow step cannot affect rate.

Apply the rate law $\text{rate} = k[\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3][\text{H}^+]$**
This tells you the slow step must involve one $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ and one $\text{H}^+$, and must not involve $\text{CN}^-$. Mechanism 1 has the slow step with $\text{CN}^-$, mechanism 2 slow step has $\text{HCN}$, mechanism 3 slow step has $\text{CN}^-$. Only mechanism 4 has slow step: $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + \text{H}^+ \to [\text{CH}_3\text{C}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3]^+$.

Match numbers to powers**
In that slow step the mole ratio is 1 mole of propanone to 1 mole of $\text{H}^+$. That matches exactly the powers 1 and 1 in the rate equation. The fast second step then adds $\text{CN}^-$ quickly to give product $\text{B}$, but it does not influence rate. That is why mechanism 4 fits.

Final answer: Proposed mechanism 4.
The slow step contains only $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ and $\text{H}^+$, the species in the rate equation, with no $\text{CN}^-$.
The stoichiometric ratio in the slow step is 1:1, corresponding to first order in each in the rate equation.

hints: Hot aqueous acid converts a $-\text{CN}$ group into a $-\text{COOH}$ group, apply this to the structure of B keeping the rest of the molecule unchanged.
walkthrough:
Spot the hydrolysis change**
Compound $\text{B}$ is $\text{CH}_3\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{CN})\text{CH}_3$, a hydroxynitrile. Hot acidic hydrolysis replaces the nitrile carbon with a carboxyl group. The $-\text{CN}$ becomes $-\text{COOH}$ plus an ammonium ion as by product.

Draw C**
Keep the central carbon with its $\text{OH}$ and two $\text{CH}_3$ groups exactly as in $\text{B}$, just swap $\text{CN}$ for $\text{COOH}$. That gives 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanoic acid, formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_3$ as required.
Final answer: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{OH})\text{COOH}$ i.e. central C bonded to $\text{OH}$, $\text{COOH}$ and two $\text{CH}_3$ groups: $\text{HO}-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2-\text{COOH}$.

hints: Convert $\text{p}K_a$ to $K_a$ using $K_a = 10^{-\text{p}K_a}$ and write the expression $K_a = [\text{H}^+]^2 / [\text{HA}]$ for a weak acid.
Solve for $[\text{H}^+]$ with $c = 0.500 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, then use $\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$, keeping at least 2 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Get $K_a$ and set up the equilibrium**
For weak acid $\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-$, $$K_a = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]} \approx \frac{[\text{H}^+]^2}{c}$$ because $[\text{H}^+] \approx [\text{A}^-]$ and dissociation is small so $[\text{HA}] \approx c$. First convert: $$K_a = 10^{-3.95} = 1.12 \times 10^{-4}$$

Calculate pH**
Substitute $c = 0.500 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$: $$[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{1.122 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.500} = 7.49 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ Then $$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(7.49 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.13$$ to 3 significant figures, well within 2 s.f. minimum.

Final answer: $K_a = 10^{-3.95} = 1.12 \times 10^{-4}$
$[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_a \times c} = \sqrt{1.122 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.500} = 7.49 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
$\text{pH} = -\log(7.49 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.13$

hints: Focus on the key property of a buffer concerning pH when something is added.
Specify what must be added in small amounts for the definition to be complete.
walkthrough:
Capture the core idea**
Picture a normal solution: one drop of strong acid and pH crashes. A buffer is special because it soaks up that added $\text{H}^+$ or $\text{OH}^-$. So start with: it resists change in pH.

Add the condition**
The definition is only complete if you say when: when small amounts of strong acid or strong base are added. Large amounts will overwhelm any buffer, so the word small matters for the mark.
Final answer: A solution that resists/minimises/opposes change in pH when small amounts of (strong) acid or base are added.

hints: Calculate moles of $\text{NaOH}$ added and initial moles of acid C, then find moles of salt formed and acid left after neutralisation.
Use $K_a = [\text{H}^+] \times [\text{salt}]/[\text{acid}]$ to solve for $[\text{H}^+]$, volumes cancel so you can use moles directly.
Convert $[\text{H}^+]$ to pH with $-\log[\text{H}^+]$, check significant figures.
walkthrough:
Work out the buffer composition**
$\text{NaOH}$ neutralises part of weak acid $\text{C}$ to its conjugate base: $$\text{HA} + \text{OH}^- \to \text{A}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Moles $\text{OH}^-$ $= 0.0200 \times 1.00 = 0.0200 \text{ mol}$, so moles conjugate base formed $= 0.0200 \text{ mol}$. Initial moles $\text{HA}$ $= 0.100 \times 0.500 = 0.0500 \text{ mol}$, so moles $\text{HA}$ left $= 0.0500 - 0.0200 = 0.0300 \text{ mol}$.

Apply the equilibrium expression**
For the buffer, $$K_a = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}$$ so $$[\text{H}^+] = K_a \times \frac{[\text{HA}]}{[\text{A}^-]} = K_a \times \frac{0.0300}{0.0200}$$ Since both are in the same total volume, moles can be used directly. With $K_a = 10^{-3.95}$: $$[\text{H}^+] = 1.5 \times 1.122 \times 10^{-4} = 1.68 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$

Convert to pH**
$$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(1.68 \times 10^{-4}) = 3.77$$ This is less acidic than $\text{p}K_a$ (3.95) because acid is in excess over salt, but still in the buffer region, which makes sense.
